fixes.explanation: Elisha turns it down. He swears by the LORD that he won't take it, and when Naaman keeps pressing, Elisha still says no (2 Kings 5:16). Friend, plenty of people would have said yes by the second push. Not Elisha.
The text never says Naaman is lame. Verse 1 calls him a mighty man of valor, but the thing working against him is leprosy. It shows up right at the end of the verse, after all the good news.

The girl says, “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy.” She's the one taken from Israel, and she's the one who points to help. Small voice, big news.

Egypt isn't anywhere in this story. The king of Aram says he will send Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel (2 Kings 5:5). That's the land the girl was taken from, and she's the one who spoke of a prophet in Samaria.

The king of Israel says, “Surely you can see that he is seeking a quarrel with me!” A quarrel is a fight. He reads a letter asking for a cure, and he tears his clothes over it. I think that was a rough moment for him.

Elisha sends a messenger instead of coming out. The messenger says, “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean.” So the instructions come second-hand. I think a man with a full set of horses and chariots might have expected a handshake.

Naaman doesn't mention a blessing from the king. What he pictured was Elisha coming out, calling on the name of the LORD his God and waving a hand over the spot. The king isn't in that picture at all.

No spot is left. After the seventh dip, his flesh “…was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean.” He went into the Jordan with leprosy and came up with skin like a little child's. I bet he checked every inch twice anyway.

Naaman doesn't ask for stones. He says, “please let me, your servant, be given as much soil as a pair of mules can carry.” His request is about soil, measured by what two mules can carry. No river rocks in this story.

Dagon doesn't come up in this story. Naaman says, “…your servant will never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD.” The only other god Naaman names is Rimmon, in the next verse.

Gehazi says, “My master has sent me to say, ‘Look, two young men from the sons of the prophets have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two sets of clothing.’…” Elisha never sent him with any such message. That's the story Gehazi tells Naaman. Friend, that's a lot of detail for a made-up errand.

Gehazi never says Elisha changed his mind. He asks for a talent of silver and two sets of clothing for two young men from the sons of the prophets. His story is built around that one specific request.

Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron (Numbers 26:59), did have leprosy once (Numbers 12:10). But that's not the name Elisha says here. He says, “…the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever!” This one is about Naaman's leprosy.
